messages.subject: Re: how to skip rows when reading in data?
messages.subject_clean: how to skip rows when reading in data?
messages.body_plain:
You can do it using a pipe connection provided you have some unix tools (eg
cygwin on Windows). For instance the unix "head -n file" command prints the
first n lines of file, so you need a way of finding the number of lines in
file. One crude way is to scan it in:

> length(scan("myfile",sep="\n")) 
[1] 50
> con <- pipe("head -49 myfile")
> scan(con,sep="\n")

More subtle is to use unix "wc -l file" to find the file length, then stick
it into the head command using `` syntax. This worked on my cygwin window

cygwin% head -`wc -l myfile | awk '{print $1-1}'` myfile

but when I tried to put it into a pipe connection, I got an error dialog
box. Anyone know why?

con <- pipe("head -`wc -l myfile | awk '{print $1-1}'` myfile")
scan(con,sep="\n") # gives an error dialog box!

(Windows 2000/Splus 6.0.3)

Nick Ellis

messages.subject: quantile smoothers
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the responses to my query regarding quantile
smoothers.  The responses are summarized below.

Ed Malthouse

------------------------------------------------------------------------

>From Andy Liaw

Using Prof. Koenker's rq library, you can do quantile regression.
Using
splines as predictors, you can do a smooth quantile regression.

Here's a function courtesy of Prof. Koenker, which trace out various
quantile curves.

smoothrq.plot <- function(x, y, ...) {
  plot(x, y, ...)
  taus <- 1:99/100
  X <- bs(x,knots = quantile(x), intercept=T)
  X[is.na(X)] <- 0
  z <- seq(min(x),max(x),length=200)
  Z <- bs(z,knots = quantile(x), intercept = TRUE)
#fit_matrix(0,ncol(X),length(taus))
  k <- 0
  for(tau in taus) {
    k <- k + 1
    fit[,k] <- rq(X, y, tau, int = FALSE, ci = FALSE)$coef
    lines(z,Z %*% fit[,k])
  }
}

--------------------------------------------------------------------
>From Tim Hesterberg

On statlib, http://lib.stat.cmu.edu/S/, is:

quantreg
      Routines to compute quantile regressions including analogues of
      trimmed means for the linear model.  Updated version contains
      new functions implementing new forms of rank tests for linear
      models based on the dual quantile regression
      process. (roger at ysidro.econ.uiuc.edu)[23/Aug/91] [1/Jun/95](48
     kbytes)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
>From Leonid Gibiansky

At one point when I needed this, I used a quick and dirty multi-step
(not
too general) procedure:
1. Found mean line (lowess, etc.)
2. Separated all points into two sets that lie above and below the
mean line
3. Found the mean of the upper and the lower halves, thus creating 25 and
75th percentiles.
Leonid

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
>From Bert Gunter

I know that this has been discussed in the literature, I think by Koenker
and Bassett. So you might try a literature search (something with "weighted
quantile estimation", maybe). You should also try checking the S and R
archives, as I suspect there's something there (try looking for something to
do with weighted quantile estimation).

messages.subject: Periodic loess fits?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Splusers, I have run across the following problem several times and
hope to find a solution.

I have data collected monthly for some number of years.  I would like to
depict the seasonal pattern, as well as changes in the seasonal pattern
that occurred after an event in the middle of the record.  So I have
plotted the data by month using different symbols for pre- and post-event
data.  Now I would like to fit loess curves to each set of data (pre- and
post), but that is illogical because the data for December and January
should be close together, whereas on an ordinary plot they are distant.  So
what I really want is a loess curve calculated as if in circular
coordinates.  I could do it by replicating the data and changing the months
in the replicated data (e.g., 12 to 0, 11 to -1, plus 1 to 13, 2 to 14) to
force a fit, but that seems fudgy.  Sine + Cosine fits with a year period
would work if the data were shaped like that but they are not.

Here is what the data look like (Category is 0 through 1987, 1 after):

Year    Month   Category  Data
1975    1       0               1.2
1975    2       0               2.9
.
.
1987    12      0               5.5
1988    1       1               0.3
.
.
2001    12      1               0.7

So the question is how to fit a loess (or similarly unconstrained curve) to
these data to illustrate/draw attention to both the seasonal pattern (i.e.,
how Data change by Month) and the change in pattern starting in 1988 (i.e.,
how Data change by Month differently after than before the event).

Any ideas?

Thank you.

Wim Kimmerer

Dear Tristan,

The error occurs because deparse(substitute(x)) returns the *name* of the 
variable given as the argument x -- that is, a character string (and 
likewise for y). You could do something like

        temp <- summary(eval(parse(text = paste('lm(', deparse(substitute(x)),

                '~', deparse(substitute(y)),', na.action = na.exclude)')), 
local = sys.parent(1)))

Maybe someone else can think of something simpler. Frankly, this seems like 
a lot of trouble to calculate a multiple correlation.

I hope that this helps,
 John

messages.subject: Answers to: Subsetting lists
messages.body_plain:
OK, it was probably a dumb question, but I really couldn't find the answer.
 Thanks very much to:

Brad Biggerstaff
Sundar Dorai-Raj
Ted) Wright
Deb Carlson
Sarah Goslee
Ken Newman
Phil Spector
Andy Liaw
Jingshan Zhang
James Holtman
Bill Dunlap
Don MacQueen
Sam Buttrey

and probably some others to follow.  And the prize for most helpful answer
goes to......
Phil Spector:
  The important thing to understand about subscripting in Splus is that
single square brackets always return an object of the same mode as the
object which is being subsetted, and double square brackets return an object
of the same mode as the part of the object which is being subscripted.  So for
vectors and matrices, there's no difference:

with second prize tied between Sarah Goslee and Sam Buttrey:

There's a difference between [[ and [ 
You need to use x[1:2] which returns those components
as a list rather than extracting them from the list.

With a list there are two kinds of subset. With single square brackets you
get the elements of the list. With double square brackets, you get the
contents of the elements. So in your example x[2] is a list containing a
vector, x[[2]] is the vector itself.

Bill Dunlap of Insightful would have won a prize for his answer except for
the error about the error at the end.  According to the PM, if x is a list,
a vector of indices within the double brackets gives the element(s)
returned by selecting the element corresponding to the first index, then
the element of THAT corresponding to the second, and so forth.  

Bill's answer:
x[...] returns a list containing the elements specified by the ...
arguments.  x[[...]] returns the element itself (not in a list),
hence the ...  must specify one element.  x[[1:2]] and x[[c(3,2)]]
ought to give an error message, not an answer.

But no: for example:
p <- list(a=letters[1:2], b="I got", c="Nothing")
> p[[1:2]]
[1] "b"
> p[[1:3]]
[1] ""

FYI, I was looking for:
cat(p[2:3])
"I got" "Nothing"> 

Wim

messages.subject: Re: Beta-binomial rv generator
messages.body_plain:
One simple technique is to make use of the fact that the beta-binomial is a
mixture of binomial and beta distributions.  Here is a simple function to
generate beta-binomial random variables:

betabinom <- function(nsim=1, size=1, shape1, shape2) {
pmix <- rbeta(nsim, shape1, shape2)
rbinom(nsim, size, prob=pmix)
}

where "nsim" is the number of rvs that you want, "size" is the number of
bernoulli trials, and "shape1" and "shape2" are the parameters of the beta
distribution.

Hope this helps,
Ravi.

messages.subject: Re: migrating functions to S-PLUS 6
messages.body_plain:
It's related to the way apply() is implemented.  In S-plus 6, apply() first 
tries a fast compiled method, but if it doesn't like the return value of 
any of the sub-computations, it falls through to a slower method (this also 
means that apply() can call FUN more times than you might expect).  The 
fast compiled method doesn't attach names to columns, but the slower method 
does.  If you look at the code for apply you can see the following comment 
in the code for the slower method:

                        # must attach names to columns before applying FUN

                        # just in case FUN uses names of data.

The little experiment below can give you a better ideas of what is 
happening.  The fast compiled method doesn't like list return values, so 
that's how we can force use of the slow method; note that FUN gets called 
twice for the first row when using the slow method.

Possibly this could be interpreted as a bug in apply; the above comment 
from the code for apply() would suggest that apply() should pass through 
names in all cases.  However, this would probably slow things down when

messages.subject: Re: First max of a vector
messages.body_plain:
A while ago (like about 12 years ago) I was running into the problem of
needing the indices of the maximum elements of the rows (or columns) of
a matrix.  Think of this as a vectorized version of doing the calculation
repeatedly on many vectors.  I wrote the following function which calls
a Fortran subroutine (simple enough that it would be trivial to rewrite
it in C, for the large group who thinks Fortran went out with the Beatles).
Doesn't deal with NA, so if you think you might have those you could 
turn them all into -1e322 or whatever.

colmax<-function(x)
{       # return index of maximum element in each column
if(!is.matrix(x)) stop("must be a matrix")
storage.mode(x)<-"double"
.Fortran("colmax",as.integer(nrow(x)),as.integer(ncol(x)),x,
        index=rep.int(1,ncol(x)))$index
}

rowmax<-function(x)
{       # return index of maximum element in each row
if(!is.matrix(x)) stop("must be a matrix")
storage.mode(x)<-"double"
.Fortran("rowmax",as.integer(nrow(x)),as.integer(ncol(x)),x,
        index=rep.int(1,nrow(x)))$index
}

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

        subroutine colmax(n,m,x,index)
        integer n,m,index(m)
        double precision x(n,m),xmax
        if(n .eq. 1) return
        do 1 i=1,m
        xmax=x(1,i)
        do 1 j=2,n
        if (xmax .ge. x(j,i)) go to 1
        index(i)=j
        xmax=x(j,i)
   1    continue
        return
        end

        subroutine rowmax(n,m,x,index)
        integer n,m,index(n)
        double precision x(n,m),xmax
        if(m .eq. 1) return
        do 1 i=1,n
        xmax=x(i,1)
        do 1 j=2,m
        if (xmax .ge. x(i,j)) go to 1
        index(i)=j
        xmax=x(i,j)
   1    continue
        return
        end

messages.subject: Re: query on ML estimation
messages.body_plain:
Here 
is a simple example to do a standard normal regression via ML in 
R.

 

## 
Normal Regression via ML in R

 

  
normreg<-function(X,y, method='BFGS'){
    
X<-cbind(1,X)
    
neglnl<-function(theta,X,y){
        
ssq<-theta[length(theta)]
        
b<-theta[1:length(theta)-1]
        
lnl<-as.vector(-.5*log(ssq)-(.5/ssq)*(y-X%*%b)^2)
        
-sum(lnl)
        
}        

        
    
result<-optim(c(mean(y),rep(0,ncol(X)-1),var(y)), neglnl, hessian=T, 
method=method, X=X, y=y)

 

    
coef<-result$par
    
var<-solve(result$hessian)
    
se<-sqrt(diag(var))
    
zscore<-coef/se
    
pvalue<-2.0*(1.0-pnorm(abs(zscore)))
    
stderr<-sqrt(coef[length(coef)])
    
print(cbind(coef,se,zscore,pvalue))
    
print(stderr)
    print(var)
    
print(result$convergence==0)
    }

Call 
the function via something like:

 

    
normreg(cbind(reppct96,logvotes,adsgore,adsbush),reppct00)}

 

Where 
reppct96...adsbush are the list of independent variables and reppct00 is the 
dependent variable.

 

There 
are much better ways to write this, but you wanted a simple example and here it 
is.

 

Charles

to anyone who can assist.

i would like to know if anyone has come across the following type
of scenario, or what anyone's thoughts may be on this sitation
described.

if i have data in ANOVA style table format, where within column
variance is due to random error, but between column variance
is due to treatment effect only (that is, any influence of
random error has been blocked within the data gathering stage) how is such 
data best analysed in splus ???

i ask this because it is my understanding of the F statistic
that the denominator (within column variance) is an estimate
of standard error while the numerator (between column variance)
is due to treatment effect/s plus standard error.

But if, standard error is removed as a component from the
numerator, and there were no treatment effect difference,
the numerator would be effectively zero.

thus, can anova still be used in this situation in splus ??

any information would be kindly appreciated.

thanks

andrew

Dr AST Czarn

Dear Zhu,

You can make X into a one-column matrix with as.matrix(X), or into a
vector with as.vector(X). But why bother, since you can index the result
returned by table? For example, X[1] or X["0"] returns the
number of zeroes.

I hope that this helps,

 John

> 5 3 2

> I can use
> as.matrix(X) or as.vector(X), but it seems that it will only return the
> second row of X. But I also want the first row. If I use X[1] or X[ 0 ],
> then the return will be a vector.

Note that X[0] should be X["0"], since the name "0"
is a character value (see below).

> This
> is a toy example, but I am hoping that there is a simple way to extract
> the elements for my complicated simulation.

What you're interpreting as the first "row" is actually the
names of the elements in the second "row". In fact, there is
only one row. As I said in my original reply, you can extract elements
using the names. If, for some reason, you really need a matrix, you could
construct one, for example as follows:

    > X <- table(rpois(10, 1))

    > X.1 <- rbind(as.numeric(names(X)),
as.vector(X))

    > X.1

        [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] 

    [1,]    0   
1    2    3    4

    [2,]    2   
5    1    1    1

Does that do what you need?

John

messages.subject: Several problems with S-Plus 6.1 on Windows
messages.subject_clean: Several problems with S-Plus 6.1 on Windows
messages.body_plain:
We are having a series of problems with S-Plus 6.1.2 Release 1 under Windows XP 
and Win98 such as

- junk in data frames when importing certain Excel files
- system lockup when exporting certain files (especially under Win98SE)
- can't import Splus6\library\example5\exenvirn.sd2 without getting
  an error message (the import does work under Linux)
- when a 'label' attribute is added to a variable, especially
  a factor variable, the variable is no longer of the correct class

I know the last problem is because of design changes in version 4 of the S 
language which I have complained about repeatedly to no avail.  This problem is 
now causing us major headaches because of the Hmisc library's use of label 
attributes for variable labels (such as those imported from SAS).  I understand 
the occasional need for non-downward compatible changes in a system but such 
changes should not cause problems that don't have simple workarounds. [Others 
have told me about a workaround for this problem in SV4 but this would require 
major reprogramming in which one must constantly be creating new data types 
just to add attributes such as 'label' or 'comment'.]

I would appreciate a status report from Insightful about these problems and 
hearing about whether other users are having similar problems.

-- 
Frank E Harrell Jr              Prof. of Biostatistics & Statistics
Div. of Biostatistics & Epidem. Dept. of Health Evaluation Sciences
U. Virginia School of Medicine  http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to John Fox, James
Holtman, Thomas Jagger, Dimitris C. Rizopoulos, Nick Ellis, Andy Liaw, Carlisle
Thacker among others, who solved my question. 

 

Here is the summary: 

The basic
question is how to extract values of X, where 

 

X <- table(rpois(10,1))

 

To me, the
difficulty is how to get the value of the data that
was counted. The answer is to use names(X). After that, there is no problem to
convert to a matrix, for example,

 

rbind(as.numeric(names(X)), X)

 

Thanks again for so fast replies.

 

Zhu Wang

messages.subject_clean: two problems with gls, gnls, lme : (i) Does the argument singular.ok=T works when argument weights is specified in gls? (ii) problem with formula and update.gnls and update.lme
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I use 6.0.2 on Windows 2000. I have come in the last months with two problems with gls, gnls and lme:

1- the first problem was already submitted to the list: 

The argument "singular.ok=T" in the "control" argument does not seem to work if argument "weights" is also specified to gls. This seems to be the case also for gnls.

Examples: where Xd.dense and clust.dense produce a singular model.matrix

test_gls(model = tempo ~ Xd.dense + as.factor(clust.dense), control = list(singular.ok = T))

works fine, and ignores the "NA" parameters - as e.g. does glm. Note that anova(test) however cannot estimate anything on the second argument, incorporating NA values, contrary to anova.glm.

testb_gls(model = tempo ~ Xd.dense + as.factor(clust.dense), control = list(singular.ok = T),weights=varConstPower(form=~abs(fitted(.)),fixed=list(const=0.01)),verbose=T)

does not work. More precisely, it gives:

Iteration: 1

Objective: 3166.66349630788 , ms iterations: 3 

varStruct  parameters:

               power 

 0.00519758679260397

Convergence:

 beta varStruct 

    1        NA

There were 36 warnings (use warnings() to see them)

Problem in gls: Missing value where logical needed: if(max(aConv) <= tolerance) {

        break

This also happens if argument weights is completely specified - e.g. by fixing also power. This also happens on other models, with completely different data.

So my questions are:

Have I missed something? Is there a solution to remedy this?

2- the second problem:

It seems that update.gnls does not accept "directly reconstituted formulas". The same problem might exist with update.lme. The error messages are as follow:

Problem in update.gnls(mod, start = rep(0.5, st..: Argument "" is missi

ng, with no default 

Example:

j_500

k_4

mod <- gnls(y ~ mod.logit(a), params = list(a ~ X), start = c(0.5, 0.5), data = "" subset = 1:j)

update.gnls(    mod,start = rep(0.5,start10.nl[k]),params = list(formula(as.character(form10.nl[k]))))

Problem in update.gnls(mod, start = rep(0.5, st..: Argument "" is missi

ng, with no default 

But:

mod <- gnls(y ~ mod.logit(a), params = list(formula(    as.character(   form10.nl[k]))), start = rep(0.5,start10.nl[k]), data = "" subset = 1:j)

works fine, as well as:

toto_formula(as.character(form10.nl[k]))

update.gnls(    mod,start = rep(0.5,start10.nl[k]),params =list(toto)).

Is there a solution to this problem?

Thanks very much in advance.

Friendly,

PS: I join the data to this mail as well as the listing for the function mod.logit:

"mod.logit" = function(a)

{

        .expr1 <- exp(a)

        .expr2 <- 1 + .expr1

        .expr3 <- .expr1/.expr2

        .value <- .expr3

        .actualArgs <- match.call()["a"]

        if(all(unlist(lapply(as.list(.actualArgs), is.name)))) {

                .grad <- array(0, c(length(.value), 1), list(NULL, "a"))

                .grad[, "a"] <- .expr3 - ((.expr1 * .expr1)/(.expr2^2))

                dimnames(.grad) <- list(NULL, .actualArgs)

                attr(.value, "gradient") <- .grad

        }

        .value

}

messages.subject: Re: Correlation with many missing values
messages.body_plain:
>I have a series of variables with many missing values and I would like to
>correlate these variables between them. If I use the code (I'm using Splus
>v. 6.3 for windows): 
>
>cor(dataset, na.method="available")  
>
>I've got many correlations outside the range -1 to 1. This result doesn't
>change if  I do it pair by pair. 
>Have you got any suggestion to force the results within -1 and 1? 

(1) Use the EM estimate, based on the multivariate normal model:
        library("missing")
        sigma <- paramIter( emGauss(dataset), expand=T)$sigma
        std <- sqrt(diag(sigma))
        sigma / (std * rep(std, each=length(std)))      

See the discussion in help(cor) about missing values.

(2) You may be thinking of pairwise computation, omitting rows with
    either variable missing, e.g.
        cor( data[,1:2], na.method="omit")
I do not recommend this.  While the individual correlations are within
the range [-1,1], the correlation matrix may not be positive definite.

Tim Hesterberg

balanced (with respect to the terms in the model).

balanced version of the original data frame, but I'm having some trouble
obtaining a balanced data.frame.

One idea i have is to use terms(formula( model.object.formula )) to extract
the first-order terms of the model, then manually build a data frame using

#resp: the response variable
#data: a data frame containing the covariates (not including
#resp)
All.Possible.Subsets <- function(resp, data){
        varb <- names(data)
        data$resp <- resp
        index <- powerSet(1:length(varb))[-1]
        models <- vector(length=length(index), mode="list")
        for(i in seq(along=index)){
                form <- paste("resp~", paste(varb[index[[i]]], collapse="+"))
                X <- model.matrix.default(terms.object=form, data=data)
                if(qr(X)$rank < dim(X)[2]) form <- "resp~1" #preventing
singularities
                models[[i]] <- lm(formula=form, data)
        }
        library(MASS)
        res <- lapply(models, function(x, data) {out <-
summary.lm(x);c(out$sigma, out$r.squared, extractAIC(x)[2],
extractAIC(x, k=log(nrow(data)))[2])}, data=data)
        results <- matrix(unlist(res), ncol=4, byrow=T)
        dimnames(results) <- list(unlist(lapply(models, function(x)
{paste(formula(x))[3]})), c("sigma", "R^2", "AIC", "BIC"))
        return(results)
}

#below are the powerSet function and the version of MASS library
that I use in my function.
########################

powerSet <- function(x) {
        if(length(x) == 0)
                return(vector(mode(x), 0))
        x <- sort(unique(x))
        K <- NULL
        for(m in x)
                K <- rbind(cbind(K, F), cbind(K, T))
        apply(K, 1, function(x, s) s[x], s = x)
}

# MASS library for Venables & Ripley (2002) version 7.0

messages.subject: Summary: Hexadecimal to decimal conversion
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Samuel Buttrey, Bill Dunlap and Chuck Taylor for responding with
their functions, and to Patrick Burns for pointing out that S Poetry has
code to achieve this. If you are interested in their complete responses,
contact me directly.

Here is Samuel Buttrey's code:

> unhex (c("12", "1a", "a", "ffFF", "000009"))
[1]    18    26    10 65535     9

"unhex" <- function(vec)
{
        #
        # unhex: function to convert a string of hex values to decimal.
        # Argument: vec, vector of character strings.
        #       
        # Set up vector of hex values. Also set up names (0-9, a-f), saving
them 
        # for efficiency. Give the names to the values. Set up the output
vector.
        hex.vals <- 0:15
        nm <- c(0:9, letters[1:6])
        names(hex.vals) <- nm
        out <- numeric(length(vec))
        for(i in 1:length(vec)) {
                #
                # For each element in the vector, downshift it, break it
into its constituent
                # letters, and reverse the letters. Look up the letters in
hex.vals and multiply
                # the resulting number by 16^(that letter's position minus
one).
                #
                vec.i <- casefold(vec[i])
                chars <- rev(substring(vec.i, 1:nchar(vec.i),
1:nchar(vec.i)))
                if(any(!is.element(chars, nm))) {
                        warning("At least one element is illegal")
                        out[i] <- NA
                }
                else out[i] <- sum(hex.vals[chars] * 16^(-1 +
1:length(chars)))
        }
        #
        # Return. All is well.
        #
        out
}

My query:

In S-PLUS 6.1 for Windows, how can I convert a hexadecimal value to its
decimal equivalent? I didn't find any functions that I can call to do this.
Is there a particular library that I am supposed to be using? Didn't think
it was worth reinventing the function if someone else has already done it!

Calvin

messages.subject: proc mixed and lme
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm working in splus version 6.0 Release 1 for Linux 2.2.12 : 2000.

I have a SAS proc mixed program that performs a mixed effects analysis and
would like to do the same in splus using lme (nlme package version 3.3.1),
but do not seem to be able to reproduce the sas model.  Here's the sas
model:

proc mixed data=co2 method=ML;
        class date trmt ring collar;
        model lnflux = sin cos sin*trmt cos*trmt trmt;
        random date ring;
run;

This estimates one variance component for each of date, and ring.  There
are 70 dates so I get 70 BLUPS for date, 6 rings and
6 corresponding BLUPS.  Fine.

Now in splus I try to do the same using lme in splus.  Here's my attempt:

> fit.lme<- lme ( log(co2flux + 1) ~ sin(2*pi*julian/365) +
+                 cos(2*pi*julian/365) + trmt:sin(2*pi*julian/365) +
+                 trmt:cos(2*pi*julian/365) + trmt,
+                 data = co2.dat,
+                 random = list(date= ~1, ring=~1),
+                 method="ML")

I get a variance component for date, but now I get a variance component
for ring %in% date.  So I get 70 BLUPS for date and 70*6=420 BLUPS for
ring%in$date.  I just want 70 for date and 6 for ring.

Next in proc mixed, I add a nested random effect to the previous model.

proc mixed data=co2 method=ML;
        class date trmt ring collar;
        model lnflux = sin cos sin*trmt cos*trmt trmt;
        random date ring collar(ring);
run;

Again, I get one component for date and one for ring and, now, one for
collar within ring.  There are 12 collars in each of 6 rings so I get 72
BLUPS for collar within ring.  Fine.

In lme, I try random = list(date= ~1, ring=~1, collar~1), but this gives
one component for each of date, ring%in%date, and collar%in%ring%in$date,
which is not what I want.  I want date, ring, and collar%in%ring, but
can't seem to figure out how to control nesting in lme.

Your help is appreciated.

jarrett

To merge two data frames, both need to have at least one
extra column in addition of the ones used in the by argument:

spcode.sfr$dummy<-rep(0,nrow(spcode.sfr))

three possibilities:

need to convert both using as.character.  Factors drive me crazy,
 but
basically they are represented by integers (e.g., 1 for the first value,
etc) which saves storage space and is also more efficient when they are
used as categorical variables.  However, in this case if BOTH are factors
there is no reason to assume they have the same coding.
2. I have had trouble merging unless BOTH x and y are actually data frames
having two or more columns.  I can't see any reason for this and the Help
file says "anything that can be converted to data frames".  I get around
this by putting dummy data in a second column to keep a data frame format,
e.g.,
merge (.... data.frame(smk99[22:25], dummy=22:25])

assume that was just an error in transcription.

messages.subject: Re: Splus and C question
messages.body_plain:
To pass an Splus matrix to C, and then use it within C as a matrix, you
need to establish indexing.  The example below is taken from the survival
library.
   coxph.fit calls the C routine coxfit2 as
   
            coxfit <- .C("coxfit2", iter=as.integer(maxiter),
                   as.integer(n),
                   as.integer(nvar), stime,
                   sstat,
                   x= x[sorted,] ,
                   etc...
where dim(x) = c(n, nvar).  

The relevant code from coxfit2.c is below (every blank line below should
have "..." perhaps, to show that I've skipped over material not relevant to
this example).  The S_dmatrix routine is part of Splus.

/*
** here is a cox regression program, written in C
**  the input parameters are
**
**       maxiter      :number of iterations
**       nused        :number of people
**       nvar         :number of covariates
**       time(n)      :time of event or censoring for person i
**       status(n)    :status for the ith person    1=dead , 0=censored
**       covar(nv,n)  :covariates for person i.
**                        Note that S sends this in column major order.
......

double **S_dmatrix(double*, int, int);

void coxfit2(long   *maxiter,   long   *nusedx,    long   *nvarx, 
             double *time,      long   *status,    double *covar2, 

    int     nused, nvar;
    double **covar;
    
    nused = *nusedx;
    nvar  = *nvarx;
    covar= S_dmatrix(covar2, nused, nvar);

    /*
    ** Subtract the mean from each covar, as this makes the regression
    **  much more stable
    */
    for (i=0; i<nvar; i++) {
        temp=0;
        for (person=0; person<nused; person++) temp += covar[i][person];
        temp /= nused;
        means[i] = temp;
        for (person=0; person<nused; person++) covar[i][person] -=temp;
        }

        
-----
 Last: I only work on one machine platform.  Looking at S Programming by
Venables and Ripley, I see that some other internal S routines have name
differences in Windows and R.  Is it S_dmatrix, Sdmatrix, just dmatrix, ...?
Someone else will have to answer that.

        Terry Therneau

messages.body_plain:
Dorothean Professor in Computer Science at the University of Vermont
====================================================================

The College of Engineering and Mathematics at the University of
Vermont invites applications for the Dorothean Professorship (at the
Full Professor or Associate Professor level) in Computer Science,
commencing with the 2003-04 academic year.  Tenure will be sought at
time of appointment.

The University of Vermont, one of the top public national
universities, is located in Burlington, Vermont.  It offers a
supportive research environment in a relatively small city that
repeatedly has drawn national attention for offering a high quality of
life.  The greater Burlington area includes 125,000 people, and is
situated on the shores of Lake Champlain between the Green Mountains
of Vermont and the Adirondack Mountains of New York.  Burlington and
the surrounding area provide an environment rich in cultural and
recreational activities.  The Department of Computer Science offers
programs in the College of Engineering and Mathematics and the College
of Arts and Sciences, as well as a joint program with the School of
Business Administration.

Our existing faculty in Computer Science are involved in the forefront
of research in knowledge and data engineering (such as data mining,
database systems, pattern recognition, and knowledge-based systems),
software engineering and verification (including programming
languages), and computational sciences (including computational
biology, discrete modeling, and numerical methods).  We are seeking to
complement and further strengthen our existing research and teaching
activities in these areas.  Candidates in these areas are most sought,
and candidates in any other area of computer science will also be
considered seriously.

Candidates should have a distinguished research record, hold a
doctorate in Computer Science or a closely related field, and have
broad teaching abilities and interests.  The successful applicant is
expected to (1) play a major role in departmental research initiatives
and the graduate program coordination, (2) strengthen and build
interdisciplinary bridges between the Department of Computer Science
and other departments within the University, and (3) take an active
role in teaching computer science courses.

Please send a letter of interest, a curriculum vitae, a statement of
teaching experience and interests, a statement of research interests
and aspirations to, and arrange for at least three letters of
reference to be sent to

      Chair, Dorothean Professor Search Committee,
      Department of Computer Science, 
      University of Vermont, 
      Burlington, VT 05405.  

Complete applications received by January 20, 2003 will be fully
considered.  For more information about the Department and the College
please see http://www.cs.uvm.edu or email to cssearch at emba.uvm.edu.

The University of Vermont is an Affirmative Action/Equal Opportunity
employer and encourages applications from women and members of
minority groups.

messages.subject: Re: Fine tuning graphics
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jindan,

At 02:02 AM 9/23/2002 -0500, Jindan Zhou wrote:
> Hello members!
>
>
>
> I made a simple plot as following:
>
>
>
> x <- rnorm(25)
> plot(x, type="o")
>
> the tick mark and labels for both x and y axis are plotted
> automatically, how do I get rid of the tick marks for axis?

To exert more control over the axes, suppress them in the initial plot by 
specifying axes=F, and then add them individually using axis():

    x <- rnorm(25)
    plot(x, type="o", axes=F)
    box()
    axis(1, ticks=F)
    axis(2, ticks=F)

This will give you axes without ticks, but with the tick labels. If you 
want to get rid of the tick labels as well, then just don't draw the axes:

    plot(x, type="o", axes=F)
    box()

> Suppose further I need to label each points on the chart, what is the best
> way to avoid the overlapping between the labels and lines?(Notice the plot
> type is "o"). It would be ideal if I can have all the labels right above
> the points when x > 0, and all the labels right below the points when x <
> 0.

It's not hard to check the signs of the points and raise or lower the 
position of the text accordingly, but avoiding the lines is a much harder 
problem. Unless you have a large number of points, I'd position the labels 
with the mouse, using locator() to get the coordinates. Perhaps someone 
else will figure out a more elegant solution.

I hope that this helps,
 John

messages.body_plain:
Hi, There,

 

I have some noisy time series measurements, which 
is non-stationary in the sense that we measure the temperature change during 
rapid cooling/heating phases. I want to reduce the noise (white noise and some 
small bumps, which likely be caused by bad contact during the experiments), but 
keep the temperature change at transient points as sharp as 
possible.

 

I tried smooth methods (B-spline and Lowess), they 
tend to smooth both noise and my sharp transient feature. I thought about smooth 
methods with various window width (kernel method), but it work for uneven time 
intervals and my measurements have even time intervals (5 seconds for 3 
hours).

 

I wonder how scale analysis method (wavelet) or 
frequency method (fft) could be used here? Are they equally effective? Which one

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Can any of you help me with this plot?  I am trying to plot a graph with
different scales for each axis.  However, the length of each axis being
same.

Ex: measureVect <- c(0.25,100,4.2,1200)

I would line to draw a chart with 4 points on different axes: '0.25' on
positive x-axis, '100' on positive Y-axis, ' 4.2' on negative X-axis and
'1200' on negative Y-axis. I would like to draw the graph with all axes
having the same length representing different scales having tick marks for
each axis.  And then join all these four points together with lines.

I tried the following way:

----------------------------------------------------

plot(c(0.25,0,-4.2,0,0.25),c(0,100,0,-1200,0),type="l",xaxt='n',yaxt='n',
xlab="",ylab="")
lines(c(0,0.25),c(0,0))
lines(c(0,0),c(0,100))
lines(c(0,-4.2),c(0,0))
lines(c(0,0),c(0,-1200))

x1ticks <- pretty(c(0,0.25), nint=5)
x2ticks <- pretty(c(0,4.2), nint=5)
xticks <- unique(c(-x2ticks,x1ticks))
y1ticks <- pretty(c(0,100), nint=5)
y2ticks <- pretty(c(0,1200), nint=5)
yticks <- unique(c(-y2ticks,y1ticks))
axis(1,at=xticks,labels=as.character(abs(xticks)))
axis(4,at=yticks,labels=as.character(abs(yticks)))

----------------------------------------------

With this, I can draw four lines and join them together.  But I couldn't
achieve having all different axes of same length with different scales on
each axis.

Can any of you suggest a better way of working with this problem?

Thanks,

Padma

messages.subject: Re: Strange Behavior of levels !
messages.body_plain:
The possible levels of a factor are created when it is
constructed and subsets of the variable keep the same
possible levels.  One solution would be to reconstruct
the factor.

Example:
> x <- factor(letters)
> x    
 [1] a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z
> x[1:4]
[1] a b c d
Levels (first 5 out of 26):
[1] "a" "b" "c" "d" "e"
> levels(x[1:4])   
 [1] "a" "b" "c" "d" "e" "f" "g" "h" "i" "j" "k" "l" "m" "n"
[15] "o" "p" "q" "r" "s" "t" "u" "v" "w" "x" "y" "z"
> y <- x[1:4]
> y <- factor(as.character(y))        
> y
[1] a b c d
>

Regards,
Henrik

messages.subject: Re: xlab with apply, hist
messages.body_plain:
Beth:

The apply(hist) behavior appears to be a bug. INSIGHTFUL PLEASE TAKE NOTE! I
was able to reproduce it as follows:

>x_matrix(rnorm(100),nc=10)
>apply(x[,1:4],2,hist)

## produced 6 histograms, first 2 repeated.

>apply(x,2,hist)  # produced 12 histograms! 

This appears to be some sort of interaction of apply with hist().

However the labeling problem is not a bug. In your command:
apply(data[,1:4],2,function (x) hist(x, xlab=name.cols(data[,1:4])))

the xlab argument is the same character string vector of length 4 at each
call of hist. hist() xlab needs a single character string, not 4 of them,
and so just uses the first each time. To do what you want, using a loop is
simpler and no slower, I believe:

namecol_name.cols(data[,1:4])
for(i in 1:4)hist(data[,i],xlab=namecol[i])

Cheers,

messages.subject: Re: xlab with apply, hist
messages.body_plain:
At 02:05 PM 9/23/2002 -0700, Beth Wilmot wrote:
> Dear members,
>
>
>
> S+ version 6.2 for Windows 2000
>
>
>
>
> I've created histograms with apply and have 2 questions:
>
>
>
> apply(data[,1:4],2,hist)
>
>
>
> gives me  6 histograms; the first 2 are repeated and since the x labels
> are a vector for the first 2 and all the rest  x, I changed to:

An undocumented aspect of apply() is that FUN should not have side effects 
(at least in S-plus 6).  This is because apply() first tries a fast method, 
but if FUN returns a data structure that the fast method doesn't like (I 
think it only likes vectors and matrices), the fast method fails and 
apply() goes on to use a slow method, starting at the beginning 
again.  This means that FUN can be called up to 2N times (where N is the 
number of times you might think it would be called.)  If FUN always returns 
a list, as does hist(), then it will be called N+1 times (1 time to fail in 
the fast method).

The way to get the behavior you want is either:

for (i in seq(len=dim(data[,1:4])[2])) hist(data[,1:4][,i])

OR

lapply(data.frame(data[,1:4],check.names=F,check.rows=F), hist)

I'd recommend the for loop: you're pretty unlikely to actually need to use 
a apply() instead of for when you're doing graphics, and it's much easier 
to pass arguments to the iterated function.   If you do have a task that 
can't be accomplished with a for loop, it's probably better to split your 
task into two parts, the first the computationally intensive part that 
requires the use of apply, and the second the graphics.  And anyway, the 
computational engine of S-plus 6 is significantly more memory efficient 
than earlier versions and apply() is less often required.

-- Tony Plate

messages.body_plain:
I have had this problem before and have reported it to Insightful last year.
This is, as Tony Plate said, due to a side effect due to the attempt to use
a "fast" method for apply.  A simple way to avoid this side-effect is to
make the function in apply return some value, such as follows:

    x_matrix(rnorm(100),nc=10)
    apply(x[,1:4],2,function(x) {hist(x);1})

Ravi.

messages.subject_clean: SUmmary of response re simple plotting question
messages.body_plain:
One of the fascinating things is how many different ways people solved
this.

The solution I used was provided by Andy Liaw

plot(V2, V3, type="n")
for(i in levels(V1)) {
  text(V2[V1 == i], V3[V1==i], i)
  abline(lsfit(V2[V1==i], V3[V1==i]))
}

but also given were

by Erin Hodges

xx <- xp$Cat == "A"
> xx1 <- xp$Cat == "B"
> xp1 <- lm(y~x, data=xp[xx,])
> xp2 <- lm(y~x, data=xp[xx1,])
> plot(xp1$fitted.values,type="b",pch="A",ylab=" ")
> plot(xp2$fitted.values,type="b",pch="B",ylab=" ")
> 

by Sundar Dorai Rai

options(contrasts = c(factor = "contr.treatment", order =
"contr.poly"))
df <- data.frame(y = rnorm(20) + rep(c(0, 5), each = 10),
  V1 = rep(LETTERS[1:2], each = 10),
  V2 = runif(20),
  V3 = runif(20))
df.lm <- lm(y ~ V2 + V3 + V1*V2 + V1*V3, data = df)
# estimate of slope for V1 is difference 
# between intercepts for "A" and "B"
# estimate of V1:V2 is difference
# between slopes for "A" and "B"

# predict on new data set
# setting V3 = mean(V3) marginalizes this variable
df.new <- cbind(df[, c("V1", "V2")], V3 = mean(df$V3))
df.fit <- predict(df.lm, new = df.new)

plot(df$V2, df$y, type = "n")
# this can also be accomplished with text()
points(df$V2[df$V1 == "A"], df$y[df$V1 == "A"], pch = "A")
points(df$V2[df$V1 == "B"], df$y[df$V1 == "B"], pch = "B")
# ordering makes the lines look better
df.ord <- order(df$V1, df$V2)
df <- df[df.ord, ]
df.fit <- df.fit[df.ord]
lines(df$V2[df$V1 == "A"], df.fit[df$V1 == "A"])
lines(df$V2[df$V1 == "B"], df.fit[df$V1 == "B"])

by Dimitris Rizopolous

plot(data$x, data$y, type="n", xlab="X", ylab="Y")
abline(lm(y~x, data=data[data$V=="A",]))
abline(lm(y~x, data=data[data$V=="B",]), lty=2)
text(data$x[data$V=="A"], data$y[data$V=="A"], labels="A")
text(data$x[data$V=="B"], data$y[data$V=="B"], labels="B")

and by Bert Gunter

plot(V2,V3,type='n')  ## to set up the axes but not plot
points(V2[V1=='A'],V3[V1=='A'],pch='A')
abline(lsfit(V2[V1=='A'],V3[V1=='A']),col=2)
points(V2[V1=='B'],V2[V1=='B'],pch='B')
abline(lsfit(V2[V1=='B'],V3[V1=='B']),col=3)

I have snipped some of this code, for brevity.  I believe I only
snipped parts which generated data.

Thanks to all

Peter

messages.subject: Re: Strange Behavior of levels !
messages.body_plain:
With the danger of starting a long discussion of pros and cons...

I believe that the present behaviour of [.factor is quite appropriate
from the point of view that a factor variable is defined by a its
possible levels and subsetting the variable should not change that.
However, your definition of [.factor is often more convenient.  I
suspect that this is because S-PLUS converts characters to factors far
too often.  Why not keep them as character strings and let the
modelling functions convert them? Or better; let the user define them
explicitly?

/Henrik

question. The R code I used is not automatically efficient in Splus.

I have a two column (L , T ) data frame. Column L has three levels: a, b
and c  and Column T is real valued.

   a      0.1
   a      -0.8
   a      -1.0
   b      -0.3
   b      0.7
   b      1.0
   b      0.4
   c      -0.5
   c      -1.0

My aim is to get a data frame of the form

       L    T1    T2   T3    T4   T5
       a    0.8   0.9  0.1  -0.8  -1.0
       b    -0.3  0.7  1.0   0.4   NA
       c    -0.5  -1.0  NA    NA   NA

without using a "for"  loop, but by using functions of the "apply" family
for exemple or something specific to Splus
and more efficient.

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 25 Sep 2002 09:33:27 +0200 (METDST)
Henrik Aalborg Nielsen <immhan at student.dtu.dk> wrote:

> With the danger of starting a long discussion of pros and cons...
> 
> I believe that the present behaviour of [.factor is quite appropriate
> from the point of view that a factor variable is defined by a its
> possible levels and subsetting the variable should not change that.
> However, your definition of [.factor is often more convenient.  I
> suspect that this is because S-PLUS converts characters to factors far
> too often.  Why not keep them as character strings and let the
> modelling functions convert them? Or better; let the user define them
> explicitly?
> 
> /Henrik

Long character strings with many duplicates across observations are better 
handled through factors for storage and execution efficiency.  -Frank

> 
> On Tue, 24 Sep 2002, Frank E Harrell Jr wrote:
> 
> > On Tue, 24 Sep 2002 08:22:28 +0200 (METDST
> > Henrik Aalborg Nielsen <immhan at student.dtu.dk> wrote:
> > 
> > > The possible levels of a factor are created when it is
> > > constructed and subsets of the variable keep the same
> > > possible levels.  One solution would be to reconstruct
> > > the factor.
> > > 
> > > Example:
> > > > x <- factor(letters)
> > > > x    
> > >  [1] a b c d e f g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u v w x y z
> > > > x[1:4]
> > > [1] a b c d
> > > Levels (first 5 out of 26):
> > > [1] "a" "b" "c" "d" "e"
> > > > levels(x[1:4])   
> > >  [1] "a" "b" "c" "d" "e" "f" "g" "h" "i" "j" "k" "l" "m" "n"
> > > [15] "o" "p" "q" "r" "s" "t" "u" "v" "w" "x" "y" "z"
> > > > y <- x[1:4]
> > > > y <- factor(as.character(y))        
> > > > y
> > > [1] a b c d
> > > >
> > > 
> > > Regards,
> > > Henrik
> > > 
> > > --------------------------------------------------------------------------

> > >    Informatics and Mathematical Modelling
> > >    Section for Statistics, Time Series Group

> > >    URL:    http://www.imm.dtu.dk/~han

> > > On Mon, 23 Sep 2002, Nour-Eddin Elfaouzi wrote:

> > > > Hi all;

> > > > One collegues of mine is trying to conduct tree classification using 
> > > > S-plus 
> > > > Version 6.0 Release 1 for Sun SPARC, SunOS 5.6 : 2000 where all the 
> > > > predictors 
> > > > are categoricals.
> > > > 
> > > > 
> > > > As the number of predictors' levels is limited to 32, He extracts a 
> > > > sample from 
> > > > a large table such that the limit condition is meet for all the 
> > > > predictors.
> > > > 
> > > > The problem is once tree function is called, it  stopped with a message 
> > > > saying 
> > > > that the number of levels in predictors is (still !) more that 32. This 
> > > > is of 
> > > > course not true as one can verify that by typing 
> > > > >  unique(Tab[,j])  
> > > >

> > > >

messages.subject: plotting question
messages.body_plain:
Hello all, I am trying to produce a series of plots of X1 vs Y1 from a data 
frame where X1 and Y1 do not necessarily have the same number of elements. How 
can I force pairing of X1 & Y1 so as to drop those which are not paired?

I have, for example

j <- 23
for(i in 1:9){

X1 <- date[code1==levels(code1)[j] & sid==levels(sid)[i]]
Y1 <- result[code1==levels(code1)[j] & sid==levels(sid)[i]]

plot(X1,Y1, type='b', xlab=' ', ylab='')}

which sometimes works, but often fails to 
Error in plot: Lengths of x and y must match

These are irregular time series, and the sites with modern data (1990s and on)  
have a much greater chance of being paired than earlier data (1970s and 80s). 
I've tried various for() and while() conditions, with no success. 
        
I guess I would like to force the plotting of X1 against Y1 based on their 
existence on the same date. That is, for each date both X1 and Y1 were taken, 
plot that point, and if one or the other don't exist, pass that  instance up.

Any ideas  ( I have yet to look into the whole its() concept) are greatly 
appreciated!

Michael Slattery
Geologist, Ohio EPA
Columbus OH 43215

A generally useful trick when you can do something from the menu but not 
from the command line is to do it from the menu and then look at the 
history (Menu Window->History->Display (check "in reverse order").  Nearly 
all menu actions leave the commands they executed in the history, so you 
can go in there are see what commands were used, and you can copy and use 
those commands in a script (most of the time.)

messages.subject: Multimodal ML parameter estimate distributions
messages.body_plain:
Attached is some S code which amongst other things fits a distribution 
consisting of the convolution of the exponential and Wald (the latter sometimes 
also called the Inverse Gaussian) distribution using maximum likelihood (ML). 

The convolution distribution (ExWald) has both real and complex cases, the 
latter requiring approximation by an infinite series. My main question concerns 
results from a monte carlo study on parameter estimation (see attached draft 
paper): with small samples, and even in some cases with very large samples, I 
get multimodal parameter sampling distributions. 

Does anyone know of similar cases where ML acts like this in finite samples, 
despite its asymptotic properties? Any fixes or explanations? 

Second, in implementing the infinite series approximation in S I discovered 
that it was much faster (presumably due to memory allocation costs) to 
calculate a blocks of terms in a vectorised manner. The function "uandv" does 
this, checking for convergence after each block (it can also do one larger 
block first). Is this good S style? Are there other approaches (aside from 
linking compiled code)? 

Finally, a point of etiquette; my code includes a slightly augmented version of 
vcov.nlminb from the MASS library (I augmented it to catch errors and to return 
approximate parameter estimate standard errors and correlations rather than the 
variance-covariance matrix). I will of course cite the source, and have emailed 
the author, Prof. Ripley (no reply, I suspect he is on holiday), but was 
wondering what the usual procedure is when making use of someone's S code like 
this. I intend to freely make my code available. If I was a better S programmer 
I could probably have written funciton that called vcov.nlminb, trapped the 
errors somehow and added the extra calculations, but it was easier for me just 
to modify the funtion itself.

Cheers

P.S. In answer to Weijie Cai's question on fitting the Gamma with MLE, you 
could insert the gamma density dgamma where I use, e.g. pwald. I prefer to use 
nlminb(), which allows parameter estimates to be constrained (e.g., > 0) 
although this can be achieved using ms() by reparameterization (e.g., estimate 
exp(parameter)). For the two parameter gamma (i.e., with no shift parameter) 
start points for search can be obtained from the first two moments of the 
sample: mean = shape/rate, variance = shape/rate^2, so estimate rate = 
mean/variance, shape = est(rate)*mean (see dgamma help). In my experience, and 
unlike the ExWald, MLE works well for the gamma, and other positively skewed 
distributions such as the weibull, lognormal etc, even when a shift parameter 
is added. vcov.nlminb (from the MASS library) can be used to get the parameter 
estimate variance-covariance matrix by numerical differences when objective 
function derivatives are not supplied.

messages.subject: Re: fit the MLE of gamma dist
messages.subject_clean: fit the MLE of gamma dist
messages.body_plain:
Let's 
take a bigger sample:

 

> y <- rgamma(5000, shape = 4, 
rate = 5)
> fm <- glm(y ~ 1, Gamma(link = identity))

> 
library(MASS)

> shape <- 
gamma.shape(fm)$alpha
> rate <- shape/coef(fm)
> c(shape = shape, 
rate = as(rate, 
"vector"))
    shape     rate 

 4.016532 5.028475

 

Alternatively:

 

> gm <- ms(~ -log(dgamma(y, 
shape = shape, rate = rate)), 

    start = c(shape=4, rate=5), 
trace = T)
> coef(gm)
    shape     
rate 
 4.016532 5.028475

Of 
course this is only half the story.  If you want standard errors you need 
to do a bit more work, but the information is there in the object fm and the 
output from gamma.shape(), which is part of the MASS 
library.

 

This 
is a fascinating simple problem and I could go on and on about it.  In fact 
I think I will.

 

In 
the MASS library for S-PLUS 6.x there is (courtesy of BDR) now a 
function optim() that not only optimises but optionally gets you a Hessian at 
the optimum.  So another way of finding the mle and getting an approximate 
variance matrix as well is as follows:

 

> 
fgamma <- function(par, y) 

        - sum(log(dgamma(y, 
shape = par[1], rate = par[2])))
> par <- c(shape = 4, rate = 
5)
> hm <- optim(par, fgamma, hessian = T, y = y)

> se <- 
sqrt(diag(solve(hm$hessian)))  # don't forget to invert!
> 
cbind(hm$par, 
se)
                       
se 
shape 4.016415 0.07722422
 rate 5.028294 
0.10298544

Easy 
peasy.

 

Bill Venables .

messages.subject: merge data.frames by timeDate
messages.body_plain:
Dave, I have found timeDate to be so mysterious and klunky that I have
given up on it (Splus 6.0, but I think it is the same).  Merge, graphs, and
quite a few other operations that should be straightforward give you
garbage.  I wrote a few simple functions to compute year , month, and day
(NOT as factors, which even SPlus 2000 returned for some reason, but as
numbers) and use those to merge.  A lot of my data are daily so I don't
care about the time, but I think it has something to do with time zones.
The transition between daylight time and standard time will catch you too. 

My suggestion in Splus 6.x is to avoid timeDate for most numerical operations.

Wim

messages.subject: Re: merge data.frames by timeDate
messages.body_plain:
I agree that the timeDate objects can be mysterious at first. Insightful's 
manual description of these objects is a bit confusion. And, Insightful does 
not make clear which functions operate correctly on them and which do not. For 
merging data on timeDate, I recommend creating timeSeries objects and then 
using the function seriesMerge. I don't think this works at the gui level (I 
keep bugging Insightful to improve the gui support for timeSeries objects). 
Also, you do have to be careful about time zone issues and I recommend setting 
the time zone to GMT using the options command to avoid any strangeness. In 
S-PLUS 6 for windows, the time zone of the timeDate object was set according to 
the windows regional setting. In S-PLUS 6.1, I believe the default is now GMT.

However, after figuring out how they work I found the new time series objects 
(timeDate and timeSeries) to be extremely powerful and useful, especially for 
dealing with high frequency financial data. My recent book, Modeling Financial 
Time Series with S-PLUS, Springer 2002, emphasizes the usefulness of the new 
time series objects in S-PLUS 6. See, in particular, chapter 2 on time series 
specification, manipulation and visualization.

Unfortunately, Insightful has not integrated the new timeSeries objects into 
all of the statistical fitting functions. However, you can always strip away 
the timeDate information of a timeSeries by extracting the data using the 
seriesData function. The new S+FinMetrics module I helped develop is built 
around the new timeSeries objects and all of the functions work correctly with 
timeDate and timeSeries objects.

If you work a lot with time series data, I wouldn't give up on the timeDate and 
timeSeries objects. They are extremely powerful and useful.

ez

messages.subject: dup.row.names in S+ 6.0 UNIX
messages.body_plain:
Dear List;

I noticed that S+ 6.1 is a little more lenient with duplicate row names in 
data.frames, if you use row.names(x)_c("A","A") or 
data.frame(x,row.names=c("A","A")) you get a warning but not an error.  I'm 
trying to get duplicate row names into a dataframe on S+ 6.0 on UNIX.  
row.names() will not allow duplicate names so that's out.  However 
data.frame(x,row.names=y[,1], dup.row.names=T) won't work either.  My x is a 
data.frame, my y is a dataframe containing the duplicated names I want to 
use in column 1, same number of rows as x.  I get no error but the row names 
either stay blank or they change to numbers, 1 through nrow(x) depending on 
how I coerce y (as list, vector, character, etc.).  What is the appropriate 
data type for row names in data.frame()?

Thank you for any help with this.

Phillip Stafford
Amersham Biosciences

messages.subject: Re: fit the MLE of gamma dist
messages.subject_clean: fit the MLE of gamma dist
messages.body_plain:
What 
about the fitdistr function in the MASS library (S-Plus 6.0 for Windows)?  
Seems to provide a very nice front-end to nlminb, with vcov matrix estimated 
with vcov.nlminb of MASS:

 

> 
fitdistr(y,dgamma,start=list(shape=4,rate=5))
    
shape        
rate      
  4.044972     
5.035894   
 (0.07821524) (0.1037563 )

 

(The 
exact values naturally differ from Bill's because it's a different 
sample.)

 

Brad

>   -----Original Message-----
> From: Bill.Venables at CMIS.CSIRO.AU
>   [mailto:Bill.Venables at CMIS.CSIRO.AU]
> Sent: Saturday, September 28,
>   2002 19:25 PM
> To: wjcai2001 at hotmail.com;
>   s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
> Subject: Re: [S] fit the MLE of gamma
>   dist
>
>
>
>   Let's take a bigger sample:
>
>
>
>   > y <- rgamma(5000, shape =
>   4, rate = 5)
> > fm <- glm(y ~ 1, Gamma(link =
>   identity))
>
>
>   > library(MASS)
>
>   > shape <-
>   gamma.shape(fm)$alpha
> > rate <- shape/coef(fm)
> > c(shape =
>   shape, rate = as(rate,
>   "vector"))
>     shape     rate
>
>  4.016532 5.028475
>
>
>
>   Alternatively:
>
>
>
>   > gm <- ms(~ -log(dgamma(y,
>   shape = shape, rate = rate)),
>
>       start = c(shape=4, rate=5),
>   trace = T)
> > coef(gm)
>
>   shape     rate
>  4.016532
>   5.028475
>
>
>
>   Of
>   course this is only half the story.  If you want standard errors you need
>   to do a bit more work, but the information is there in the object fm and the
>   output from gamma.shape(), which is part of the MASS
>   library.
>
>
>
>   This is a fascinating simple problem and I could go on and on
>   about it.  In fact I think I will.
>
>
>
>   In
>   the MASS library for S-PLUS 6.x there is (courtesy of BDR) now a
>   function optim() that not only optimises but optionally gets you a Hessian at
>   the optimum.  So another way of finding the mle and getting an
>   approximate variance matrix as well is as follows:
>
>
>
>   > fgamma <- function(par, y)
>
>           - sum(log(dgamma(y,
>   shape = par[1], rate = par[2])))
> > par <- c(shape = 4, rate =
>   5)
> > hm <- optim(par, fgamma, hessian = T, y = y)
>
> > se
>   <- sqrt(diag(solve(hm$hessian)))  # don't forget to invert!
> >
>   cbind(hm$par,
>   se)
>
>   se
> shape 4.016415 0.07722422
>  rate 5.028294
>   0.10298544
>
>
>   Easy peasy.
>
>
>
>   Bill Venables .
>
>
>
>
>
>
>   Bill Venables.
>
>   >     -----Original Message-----

> >     it.
> >

> >     W.Cai

messages.subject: Moran's I for residuals from a regression
messages.subject_clean: Moran's I for residuals from a regression
messages.body_plain:
I understand that spatial.cor will calculate Moran's I statistic for a set of 
spatially explicit data.  However, Cliff and Ord (1981), and Cliff et al. 
(1975) suggest that the first two moments of this statistic should be modified 
when one is trying to look for spatial autocorrelation among residuals from a 
regression as opposed to spatial autocorrelation among the values of the raw 
data themselves.  Does anyone out there have a program that will estimate the 
mean and variance of Moran's I of residuals?

Many thanks in advance

Manuela

Cliff, A. D., P. Haggett, J. K. Ord, K. A. Bassett, and R. B. Davies. 1975. 
Elements of spatial structure. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge.
Cliff, A. D., and J. K. Ord. 1981. Spatial processes - Models and Applications. 
Pion, London.

--
